CLICK. And it held.\"). Chapters 2, 8 and 9 are thin tour stops with no mini-challenge, so the second half flattens into a timeline.","facts":"The key dates and details are correct and woven into scenes: 1932, leg godt/1934, the 1947 machine, Automatic Binding Bricks, the 28 January 1958 patent, LEGOLAND in 1968 and the minifigure in 1978. The machine appears to pop out a studded brick on arrival in 1947, which compresses the timeline (Automatic Binding Bricks came in 1949). Handing the tube idea to a time-travelling child is fiction, but the True Facts list does not claim it.","age_fit":"Length (1538) is within range, and the sound words and shout-alongs suit band A. Chapter 3 wakes the children at night to \"FIRE! The workshop is on fire!\" with \"Orange flames danced in the dark\" as everything burns. That is real peril for a band where peril should be none, even though it resolves within the chapter. \"Patent\" and \"times are hard... Nobody has money\" go unexplained for a 4-year-old.","continuity":"This is a first story with no bible, and the device and catchphrase (\"Play well\") are set up and paid off consistently. However, the text contradicts itself on who is who: \"Cruz grabbed Cruz's hand\" and \"Cruz carried planks. Cruz handed out nails.\" There is also a two-Cruz exchange in the final chapter (\"'And kids who tested it all,' said Cruz\").","delight":"There is good rhythm and onomatopoeia (\"quack-clack, quack-clack\", \"CLUNK. HISSSS. POP!\", \"He pulled. It held. He shook. It held.\"), and the ending is warm. But a parent reading aloud will stumble over lines like \"Cruz grabbed Cruz's hand\" and the back-to-back Cruz dialogue. These breaks are jarring and undermine the read-aloud experience."},"caps_applied":["none"],"disqualified":false,"overall":3.3,"editor_notes":["Restore Phoenix throughout.
